entries.title: daydreams
entries.html:
i was sitting here at my desk, procrastinating by working on some llm training that i'm sure at this point is a complete and total waste of my time, when i fell asleep for a moment and his this dream, briefly:

i'm sitting at a desk, with an old, narrow staircase in front of me, like i am on the landing, and i'm watching these happy, energetic seeming people in nice clothes chit-chatting amongst themselves as the climb these stairs in front of me. Their conversations are positive and optimistic, talking about various things that are going well for them, or achievements they've made, or things they are proud of... not in a boastful or conceited way, but in a casual, interesting kind of way, the way that makes you want to hear more about whatever it is they're describing.

The symbolism is a little heavy handed. I mean really. I guess subtlety doesn't work that well on me either, it's too easy to pretend not to notice and then genuinely forget, so i guess my subconscious is switching out the surrealism and hints and indirection for acting out it's urgent messages with charades, out of desperation and frustration with my inexplicable refusal to get it.

At least, i'm assuming that's what that means.

Who knows? t's just a dream, anyway.

entries.title: polya's adage
entries.html:
This is from the foreward to the book "Combinatorial Species and Tree-Like Structures" by François Bergeron, Gilbert Labelle and Pierre Leroux and Gian-Carlo Rota (translated by Margaret Readdy):

"Advances in mathematics occur in one of two ways.

The first occurs by the solution of some outstanding problem, such as the Bieberbach conjecture or Fermat's conjecture. Such solutions are justly acclaimed by the mathematical community. The solution of every famous mathematical problem is the result of joint effort of a great many mathematicians. It always comes as an unexpected application of theories that were previously developed without a specific purpose, theories whose effectiveness was at first thought to be highly questionable.

Mathematicians realized long ago that it is hopeless to get the lay public to understand the miracle of unexpected effectiveness of theory. The public, misled by two hundred years of Romantic fantasies, clamors for some “genius” whose brain power cracks open the secrets of nature. It is therefore a common public relations gimmick to give the entire credit for the solution of famous problems to the one mathematician who is responsible for the last step.

It would probably be counterproductive to let it be known that behind every “genius” there lurks a beehive of research mathematicians who gradually built up to the “final” step in seemingly pointless research papers. And it would be fatal to let it be known that the showcase problems of mathematics are of little or no interest for the progress of mathematics. We all know that they are dead ends, curiosities, good only as confirmation of the effectiveness of theory. What mathematicians privately celebrate when one of their showcase problems is solved is Polya's adage: “no problem is ever solved directly.”

First off, what a great opening line. It's decisive, polarizing and has broad, sweeping implications that leave the reader reeling. And by the end of the few short paragraphs, we are left with the enigmatic statement in bold that is the namesake of the title of this post. It makes the reader think, "I wonder what they mean by that? It sounds intriguing, I guess I will have to read on and find out...". Love this.

entries.title: so, web frontend is (finally) pretty cool
entries.html:
...it only took about 30 or so years.

come to think of it though, that's probably decently fast for such a widely used and versatile technology.

here are some relevant neat things i found today:

  • unstorage — "A simple, small, and fast key-value storage library for JavaScript."
    Decouple your application's persistent storage needs from your storage mediums/providers. Something so obvious it doesn't even occur to us devs.
  • unicode — Is getting quite out of hand. Last time I took a look at the full codepoint list was about a year ago. There are a lot more pages now, including fun box- and pseudo-graphics-drawing glyphs. And yes, even more arrows, yay!
  • material ui — I personally am inclined to roll my own web component `customelement` subclasses for encapsulating/modularizing compound frontend ui patterns, but there are emerging some very nice, modern and clean-looking libraries of them by others who came (up with the same idea) before.

putting the web audio and music theory stuff on brief pause this week to work on...

computer vision with deep learning(!)

...or, more specifically, semantic segmentation for extracting sprites from pixel-art composite images.

I'm using (at my main man Claude's helpful suggestion) these fancy U-nets that have learnable attention gating on the skip connections (to improve performance and ability to generalize without greatly increasing the number of learnable parameters), with compound loss and something called deep supervision (which I'm personally still trying to wrap my head around) to deal with under-sized and lumpy, misshapen datasets where classes are not equally represented, because labelling images densely by hand is really tedious.

this is a project that i've had in mind for quite some time (and even tried to get started once or twice in the past, without much success). these examples i'm working off of are from the amazing artworks of eBoy studios of Los Angeles, California, whom I have nothing but the utmost admiration for. i'm happy with how the project is going... here's some sample outputs from the first training run. I expect these results to improve greatly, but they're already impressive, and would definitely save a ton of time masking and extracting such sprites by hand:

entries.title: un1tz3r0 @ 2025-09-03T01:59:00
entries.html:
laserdisc was an awesome format, ntsc or pal video, etched right on there in all its analog glory. oh the entropy, you could really feel the connection to the players up on the screen. those times are gone now. everything is digital, everything is simulated. everything is lies,  everything spies.

if it is a black box to you, then you had better believe it is spying on you. saas and paas are the most egregious offenders. not only are you locked into a subscription model, paying out the nose for life, but everything you do is watched, examined and tracked. if you think you have privacy, digitally, you're living in a dangerously out-of-touch dream world. this is not the right way to keep everyone honest.
